# De-identification in Practice {#sec-deident-practice}



Of the 2,432 patients in the
HF-HOME demographics file, 2,422
are the only person in the file with their combination of
five-digit ZIP code, date of birth, and sex, the three fields that
singled out the Weld records (@sec-deident). The file is
synthetic, but its fields behave as a real trial's do, and the
arithmetic is the same. Removing the names, record numbers, and
telephone numbers changes none of those combinations. This chapter
builds two releases of the file, one under Safe Harbor and one
that needs an Expert Determination, writes the assertions each
must pass, and then measures what both leave behind. The concepts
are in @sec-deident; here they meet the wrangling and joins of the
preceding chapters, and each claim about a release becomes a line
of code that fails when the claim is false.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Data can be either useful or perfectly anonymous but never
both.*

[Paul Ohm]{.smallcaps}, *Broken Promises of Privacy*, UCLA Law
Review (2010)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Where this chapter sits: a de-identified release is built at the Acquire stage, from the untouched raw files and before anything leaves the covered entity, with the tools of the Wrangle stage.](02c-deident-practice_files/figure-html/fig-deident-practice-pipeline-1.png){#fig-deident-practice-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Acquire.' width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'}
**Reading time.** About 25 minutes.

**You'll need.** @sec-deident for the three HIPAA pathways, the
eighteen Safe Harbor identifiers, and the four transformations;
@sec-wrangling for the single-table verbs; @sec-types for dates;
and @sec-joins for `relationship =` and `unmatched = "error"`.
The code uses:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
```

and calls `digest::digest()`, `purrr::map_chr()`, and
`stringr::str_extract_all()` with their namespaces.

**You'll be able to.**

- Produce a Safe Harbor release and a separate linkable release
  in R, with assertions that fail if an identifier survives.
- Show why a linkable release needs an Expert Determination, and
  verify that it preserves every interval it promises.
- Compute k-anonymity on a release and find the records that
  set it.
- Weigh a generalization against the analytic resolution it
  costs.
- Describe the Five Safes and say which safe a federated analysis
  or an output check addresses.
- Generate a naive synthetic release, show where it fails a
  utility check, and measure how often it still reproduces a real
  patient's unique combination of quasi-identifiers.

**Outline.**

- [Worked example: two releases of the HF-HOME demographics](#sec-deident-worked)
- [Quasi-identifiers and residual risk](#sec-deident-risk)
- [Trusted research environments](#sec-deident-tre)
- [Synthetic data and differential privacy](#sec-deident-synthetic)
:::

If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The
answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-02c.

1. A Safe Harbor release pools ages over 89 as '90+'. Why must
   it also remove the birth year of those patients?
2. A release is 1-anonymous on age, sex, and ZIP prefix. What
   does that mean, and why does a large average cell size not
   help?
3. Why does a linkable release shift each patient's dates by
   that patient's own offset, rather than shifting the whole study
   by one offset?
:::

## Worked example: two releases of the HF-HOME demographics {#sec-deident-worked}

The HF-HOME demographics file holds every kind of identifier a
real trial file does. The names, medical record numbers (MRNs,
prefixed `SYN-`), and telephone numbers (in the fictional `555-01`
exchange) are synthetic; the ZIP codes are real codes, so the
transformations behave as they would on real data; some patients
are over 89; and the generator plants three ZIP prefixes, `036`,
`059`, and `821`, that the HHS guidance lists among the 17
prefixes whose areas had 20,000 or fewer people in the 2000
Census. The regulation asks for current Census data, and the
guidance warns against relying on its 2000 list once newer data
are published; derive the list from current data before applying
this code to real data.[^zip3]

[^zip3]: The three prefixes are the ones the HF-HOME generator
    plants, not the complete restricted list. Hard-coding a list
    from memory, or from a model's answer, is how a restricted
    prefix ends up in a release.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
demographics <- read_csv(
  file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"),
  col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", zip = "c", dob = "D",
                   age = "i", .default = "c")
)
baseline <- read_csv(
  file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"),
  col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", discharge_date = "D",
                   .default = "?")
)

phi <- demographics |>
  left_join(select(baseline, patient_id, discharge_date),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error")
stopifnot(nrow(phi) == nrow(demographics))

glimpse(phi)
#> Rows: 2,432
#> Columns: 12
#> $ patient_id     <chr> "0001", "0002", "0003", "0004", "0005", "0006", "0007",…
#> $ mrn            <chr> "SYN-8298957", "SYN-7150553", "SYN-6004096", "SYN-88828…
#> $ first_name     <chr> "Elena", "Yolanda", "Dana", "Victor", "Elena", "James",…
#> $ last_name      <chr> "Patel", "Ruiz", "Fox", "Underwood", "Peña", "Morales",…
#> $ dob            <date> 1946-10-11, 1946-03-28, 1961-09-07, 1955-06-27, 1961-0…
#> $ age            <int> 77, 77, 62, 68, 62, 81, 73, 62, 91, 80, 63, 76, 57, 88,…
#> $ sex            <chr> "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M", "M", "M", "M", "M", "F", …
#> $ race           <chr> "White", "White", "White", "White", "White", "White", "…
#> $ ethnicity      <chr> "Not Hispanic or Latino", "Not Hispanic or Latino", "No…
#> $ zip            <chr> "92123", "92115", "92093", "92131", "92021", "92064", "…
#> $ phone          <chr> "(858) 555-0196", "(619) 555-0126", "(858) 555-0157", "…
#> $ discharge_date <date> 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-0…
```
:::


### The Safe Harbor release

The Safe Harbor release suppresses the direct identifiers,
replaces `patient_id` with a randomly assigned subject ID,
generalizes every date to its year, pools ages over 89 and drops
their birth year, and truncates the ZIP code to three digits,
setting the restricted prefixes to `000`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
restricted_zip3 <- c("036", "059", "821")

set.seed(20260423)
crosswalk <- phi |>
  transmute(patient_id, subject_id = sprintf("S%04d", sample(n())))

release_sh <- phi |>
  left_join(crosswalk, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(
    over_89        = age > 89,
    age            = if_else(over_89, "90+", as.character(age)),
    birth_year     = if_else(over_89, NA_integer_,
                             as.integer(format(dob, "%Y"))),
    discharge_year = as.integer(format(discharge_date, "%Y")),
    zip3           = substr(zip, 1, 3),
    zip3           = if_else(zip3 %in% restricted_zip3, "000", zip3)
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, age, birth_year, sex, race, ethnicity, zip3,
         discharge_year) |>
  arrange(subject_id)

head(release_sh)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   subject_id age   birth_year sex   race          ethnicity zip3  discharge_year
#>   <chr>      <chr>      <int> <chr> <chr>         <chr>     <chr>          <int>
#> 1 S0001      81          1944 M     Black or Afr… Not repo… 921             2025
#> 2 S0002      63          1960 F     White         Hispanic… 100             2024
#> 3 S0003      71          1953 M     Asian         Not Hisp… 921             2025
#> 4 S0004      53          1971 M     Not reported  Hispanic… 921             2024
#> 5 S0005      73          1952 M     White         Not Hisp… 920             2025
#> 6 S0006      69          1955 M     White         Hispanic… 919             2025
```
:::


The `crosswalk` stays with the covered entity, apart from the
released data and never disclosed; because the subject ID carries
no information about the patient, keeping it does not break the
Safe Harbor claim (45 CFR 164.514(c)). Sorting by `subject_id`
matters too: left in `patient_id` order, the rows would still
carry enrollment order. The cost is plain in the output: with
only the year of discharge, no interval between two of a
patient's dates can be computed.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
State the Safe Harbor conditions as assertions. The chunk prints
counts only if every condition holds.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
direct <- c("patient_id", "mrn", "first_name", "last_name", "dob",
            "zip", "phone", "discharge_date")

stopifnot(
  nrow(release_sh) == nrow(phi),
  !any(direct %in% names(release_sh)),
  !any(vapply(release_sh, inherits, logical(1), "Date")),
  all(is.na(release_sh$birth_year[release_sh$age == "90+"])),
  !any(release_sh$zip3 %in% restricted_zip3),
  !anyDuplicated(release_sh$subject_id)
)

c(aged_90_plus = sum(release_sh$age == "90+"),
  zip3_set_to_000 = sum(release_sh$zip3 == "000"))
#>    aged_90_plus zip3_set_to_000 
#>             127              63
```
:::


127 patients are pooled as '90+', and
63 patients have their ZIP prefix
set to `000`. The assertions check structure, not risk: they
confirm that the eighteen categories are gone, which is all Safe
Harbor promises.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Pooling ages over 89 and keeping the birth year undoes the
pooling.** A release with `age = "90+"` and `birth_year = 1931`
beside a discharge year of 2025 states the age exactly. Safe
Harbor removes 'any date element, including the year' that would
reveal an age over 89, which is why `birth_year` is set to `NA`
for those patients above, and why the assertion checks it. The
same leak runs through any pair of retained columns whose
difference is an age.
:::

### The Expert Determination release

The second release keeps what a longitudinal analysis needs. It
replaces the MRN with a salted hash, so that visits arriving in
later extracts link to the same key without a lookup table, and
shifts each patient's dates by one random per-patient offset,
preserving intervals while hiding the calendar dates. The salt is
read from an environment variable, so that it never enters the
repository; the fallback string exists only so that the book
renders.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
link_key <- function(mrn, salt) {
  purrr::map_chr(paste0(salt, mrn),
                 \(x) digest::digest(x, algo = "sha256",
                                     serialize = FALSE)) |>
    substr(1, 16)
}
salt <- Sys.getenv("HFHOME_SALT", "demo-salt-not-for-real-data")

set.seed(20260424)
offsets <- phi |>
  transmute(patient_id,
            shift = sample(-180:180, n(), replace = TRUE))

release_ed <- phi |>
  left_join(offsets, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(
    link_key          = link_key(mrn, salt),
    age               = if_else(age > 89, "90+", as.character(age)),
    discharge_shifted = discharge_date + shift,
    zip3              = substr(zip, 1, 3),
    zip3              = if_else(zip3 %in% restricted_zip3, "000", zip3)
  ) |>
  select(link_key, age, sex, race, ethnicity, zip3,
         discharge_shifted) |>
  arrange(link_key)

head(release_ed)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   link_key         age   sex   race            ethnicity zip3  discharge_shifted
#>   <chr>            <chr> <chr> <chr>           <chr>     <chr> <date>           
#> 1 0000ca0fc3c39ffc 69    M     Asian           Not repo… 921   2024-04-25       
#> 2 00157a1c90202143 74    M     Not reported    Not Hisp… 921   2024-09-24       
#> 3 003d07eddc0c7efc 82    F     Multiple        Not Hisp… 921   2023-10-25       
#> 4 005bd24f049e2156 73    F     White           Not repo… 920   2024-08-14       
#> 5 006fdf7aaa7d4aed 84    F     Black or Afric… Not Hisp… 919   2025-01-12       
#> 6 007eed041fbc6a1c 87    F     White           Hispanic… 921   2024-03-24
```
:::


Neither feature of this release is Safe Harbor. The `link_key`
is a one-way hash: the same MRN always produces the same key, so
a patient's records link across extracts, and the key cannot
feasibly be reversed provided the salt stays secret. But it is
derived from the MRN, which is exactly what 164.514(c) forbids of
a re-identification code, and anyone holding the salt can
regenerate every key from a list of record numbers. The shifted
discharge date is still a full date, finer than the year Safe
Harbor allows. A release like this one is de-identified only if a
qualified expert documents that the retained detail leaves the
risk of re-identification very small.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Release the visits through the same key and offsets, and confirm
three things: the keys are unique, every visit links to a patient
in the release, and the shifted dates reproduce every recorded
interval exactly.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
visits <- read_csv(
  file.path(hf_dir, "visits.csv"),
  col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", visit_date = "D",
                   visit_day = "i", .default = "c")
)

visits_ed <- visits |>
  left_join(select(phi, patient_id, mrn), by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(offsets, by = "patient_id",
            relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  transmute(link_key = link_key(mrn, salt), visit_type,
            visit_shifted = visit_date + shift)

linked <- visits_ed |>
  left_join(release_ed, by = "link_key",
            relationship = "many-to-one", unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(day = as.integer(visit_shifted - discharge_shifted))

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(release_ed$link_key),
  identical(linked$day, visits$visit_day),
  any(vapply(release_ed, inherits, logical(1), "Date"))
)
```
:::


The last assertion is deliberate: this release *does* contain a
full date, so the Safe Harbor check above would fail on it, as it
should.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Ask for both releases at once, so that the model has to keep the
labels apart.

> **Context.** A trial file has the columns `patient_id`, `mrn`,
> `first_name`, `last_name`, `dob`, `age`, `sex`, `race`,
> `ethnicity`, `zip`, `phone`, and a separate table gives
> `discharge_date` by `patient_id`. I will test your code on
> synthetic rows only.
>
> **Constraints.** R with `dplyr` and the native pipe. Write two
> functions. `release_safe_harbor()` suppresses direct
> identifiers, assigns a random subject ID and returns the
> crosswalk separately, keeps dates as years only, pools ages
> over 89 and removes their birth year, and truncates ZIP codes
> to three digits, setting prefixes from a `restricted_zip3`
> argument to `000`; do not supply the list of prefixes.
> `release_linkable()` replaces the MRN with a salted SHA-256
> hash, the salt read from an environment variable, and shifts
> all of a patient's dates by one random offset. Label the second
> 'requires Expert Determination', never 'Safe Harbor'.
>
> **Criteria.** List your assumptions before the code. Neither
> output may contain a direct identifier; the first may contain
> no `Date` column.

*Failure mode.* The model calls the hashed or shifted release
'Safe Harbor', derives the subject ID from the MRN, hard-codes a
salt, forgets the birth year of patients over 89, or invents a
list of restricted ZIP prefixes. *Check.* Run both functions on
`phi` and apply the two Verification chunks above unchanged; then
search the code for a string literal assigned to the salt and for
any ZIP prefix typed into it.
:::

### Exercises

1. Free-text fields defeat column-based de-identification. Give
   five HF-HOME patients a synthetic clinical note that mentions
   their own name, and one note that mentions a relative, then
   flag the identifiers with a dictionary built from the
   structured name columns. Which identifier does the dictionary
   miss, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
noted <- phi |>
  slice(1:5) |>
  mutate(notes = c(
    paste(first_name[1], last_name[1], "seen; weight up 2 kg."),
    "Patient reports improvement since discharge.",
    paste0("Discussed diuretic dose with Ms. ", last_name[3], "."),
    "Daughter Sarah will manage medications at home.",
    paste(first_name[5], "declined the day-7 visit.")
  ))

known <- unique(c(phi$first_name, phi$last_name))
pattern <- paste0("\\b(", paste(known, collapse = "|"), ")\\b")

flagged <- noted |>
  mutate(found = stringr::str_extract_all(notes, pattern)) |>
  select(notes, found)
flagged
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   notes                                           found    
#>   <chr>                                           <list>   
#> 1 Elena Patel seen; weight up 2 kg.               <chr [2]>
#> 2 Patient reports improvement since discharge.    <chr [0]>
#> 3 Discussed diuretic dose with Ms. Fox.           <chr [1]>
#> 4 Daughter Sarah will manage medications at home. <chr [0]>
#> 5 Elena declined the day-7 visit.                 <chr [1]>

stopifnot(lengths(flagged$found)[4] == 0)
```
:::


The dictionary catches the patients' own names because they are
already in a structured column of the same table. It misses
'Sarah' in the fourth note, a relative's name that appears in no
column, and it would equally miss a referring physician, an
employer, or a misspelling. A structured column has a fixed
domain, so one rule handles every value; free text has no domain,
and detection becomes a recall problem with no upper bound. That
is why regulated workflows usually suppress free text rather than
try to clean it.
:::

2. A colleague proposes one study-wide offset in place of
   per-patient offsets, 'to keep it simple'. Shift every HF-HOME
   discharge date by a single random offset, then show that
   knowing one patient's true discharge date recovers every
   patient's.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(4)
one_shift <- sample(-180:180, 1)
shifted <- phi |>
  transmute(patient_id, true_date = discharge_date,
            shifted_date = discharge_date + one_shift)

known_row <- shifted[1, ]
recovered <- shifted$shifted_date -
  (known_row$shifted_date - known_row$true_date)

stopifnot(identical(recovered, shifted$true_date))
sum(recovered == shifted$true_date)
#> [1] 2432
```
:::


All 2432 dates are recovered from one. A single offset
preserves the differences *between* patients, so a single known
date, from a news report, a social-media post, or the adversary's
own admission, anchors every other. Per-patient offsets break
that chain, at the cost of the between-patient calendar
relationship, which is why the worked example draws one offset per
patient. Even per-patient offsets leave season roughly intact
when the range is narrow, and that is part of what an Expert
Determination has to weigh.
:::

## Quasi-identifiers and residual risk {#sec-deident-risk}

Neither release guarantees that the combinations that survive are
shared by more than one person. The HF-HOME file reproduces
Sweeney's arithmetic before any transformation:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
alone <- function(d, ...) d |> count(...) |> filter(n == 1) |> nrow()

c(patients = nrow(phi),
  unique_zip_dob_sex = alone(phi, zip, dob, sex))
#>           patients unique_zip_dob_sex 
#>               2432               2422
```
:::


2422 of 2432 patients are
unique on five-digit ZIP code, date of birth, and sex, the three
fields the Weld records kept.

### k-anonymity

The simplest formal tool is [**k-anonymity**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-k-anonymity) [@sweeney2002kanonymity]:
a dataset is k-anonymous on a set of quasi-identifiers if every
combination of their values that appears is shared by at least
$k$ records, so that no individual is distinguishable from at
least $k - 1$ others. Achieving a target $k$ is a matter of
generalizing (coarsening age into bands, ZIP codes into prefixes)
and suppressing (removing the rare rows) until the condition
holds. Refinements such as l-diversity and t-closeness address
weaknesses that k-anonymity alone does not; the `sdcMicro`
package implements these methods for R [@templ2015sdcmicro].


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cells <- release_sh |> count(age, sex, zip3)

c(k = min(cells$n), patients_alone = sum(cells$n == 1))
#>              k patients_alone 
#>              1            173
```
:::


The Safe Harbor release is 1-anonymous on age, sex,
and ZIP prefix: 173 patients are alone in their
cell. Safe Harbor removed every listed identifier and certified
nothing about the remainder, which is the gap Expert
Determination exists to fill.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A release can pass every Safe Harbor check and still single
people out.** The assertions in @sec-deident-worked are structural
checks: they confirm that identifiers are absent, not that the
remainder is safe. Safe Harbor also requires that the covered
entity have no actual knowledge that the rest could identify
someone, and a team that has just counted 173
unique patients may no longer meet that condition for a public
release. Compute $k$ before you describe any release.
:::

The practical lesson is that de-identification reduces risk; it
is not a binary state. Your contribution as the statistician is
to quantify the residual risk and to match the transformation to
the sensitivity of the data and the openness of the release.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The Safe Harbor release has 2432
rows, and the average cell on age, sex, and ZIP prefix holds
5.7 patients. A colleague concludes the
release is safe. What is wrong with the reasoning?

**Answer.** $k$ is a minimum, not an average. One patient alone
in a cell is identifiable whatever the average, and the release
has 173 of them. Generalization helps only when
it merges the rarest cells, so the useful question is never 'how
coarse are my bands' but 'who is alone'.
:::

### Exercises

3. Recompute $k$ and the number of patients alone on the Safe
   Harbor release after replacing exact age with the bands under
   50, 50 to 59, 60 to 69, 70 to 79, 80 to 89, and 90+. Then drop
   `zip3` as well. How much does each step buy, and what does
   each cost?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
banded <- release_sh |>
  mutate(age_band = if_else(
    age == "90+", "90+",
    as.character(cut(suppressWarnings(as.integer(age)),
                      c(0, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90), right = FALSE))
  ))
stopifnot(!anyNA(banded$age_band))

k_summary <- function(d, ...) {
  cells <- count(d, ...)
  c(k = min(cells$n), alone = sum(cells$n == 1))
}

rbind(
  exact_age = k_summary(banded, age, sex, zip3),
  age_bands = k_summary(banded, age_band, sex, zip3),
  bands_no_zip = k_summary(banded, age_band, sex)
)
#>               k alone
#> exact_age     1   173
#> age_bands     1    21
#> bands_no_zip 21     0
```
:::




Banding age reduces the patients alone from 173
to 21 but leaves $k$ at 1:
every patient still alone lives outside the San Diego prefixes,
where so few patients share a prefix that a band cannot rescue
them. Dropping the prefix raises $k$ to
21. Each step costs analytic resolution: age
bands cost any analysis that uses age as continuous, and dropping
geography costs any adjustment for site or region. Suppressing
the few rows in the rarest cells would raise $k$ at a smaller
cost, and that trade is the kind an Expert Determination
documents.
:::

## Trusted research environments {#sec-deident-tre}

An Expert Determination release still leaves the file in
@sec-deident-worked, and every file that leaves a covered entity is
a file that can be lost, copied, or matched against another
dataset by someone the entity never agreed to trust. Some data
cannot accept that risk at any level of generalization: a rare
diagnosis, a small catchment area, or a sponsor's contractual
limits on where the data may sit. The remedy is not a better
release but no release at all. If HF-HOME's files could never
leave the hospital's own systems, the statistician still has to
produce a result, and a trusted research environment (TRE) is
where that happens: a controlled system that lets approved
analysts run approved code against the data in place, so that only
the output, never the rows, crosses the boundary.

### The Five Safes

TREs are usually organized around the **Five Safes**, a framework
for data access first set out by Desai, Ritchie, and Welpton
[-@desai2016fivesafes]. Each 'safe' is a separate control, and a
breach of any one undoes the protection the other four provide.

| Safe | Governs | HF-HOME example |
|---|---|---|
| Safe data | How identifiable the data are before anyone touches them | The Safe Harbor and Expert Determination transformations of @sec-deident-worked, applied even inside the TRE |
| Safe projects | Whether this analysis, by this analyst, is an approved use of the data | An IRB- or sponsor-approved protocol naming the 30-day composite outcome as the question, not an open-ended browse |
| Safe people | Whether the analyst is trained and accountable | Training on the data use agreement, a signed confidentiality undertaking, a login tied to one person |
| Safe settings | Whether the technical environment can leak data | No internet access from the analysis session, no USB ports, no copy-paste out of the remote desktop |
| Safe outputs | Whether what leaves the environment could still identify someone | The suppression check later in this section, applied before a table, a figure, or a coefficient leaves |

: The Five Safes, as a TRE applies them to an analysis of
HF-HOME. {#tbl-deident-five-safes}

Safe Harbor and Expert Determination are entirely about the first
row; a TRE adds the other four, which is why data judged too
sensitive to de-identify for an open release can still be analyzed
under access controls that de-identification alone does not
supply. The two are complements, not alternatives: a TRE is safer
still when the data inside it are also de-identified, because safe
settings and safe people reduce the chance of a leak, not its
consequence if one occurs.

### Federated analysis: the model goes to the data

A single TRE solves the problem for one site. A multi-site trial
raises it again, because combining patient-level data from five
hospitals into one file recreates exactly the export risk a TRE
exists to avoid, now five times over. **Federated analysis**
inverts the usual flow: the analysis code travels to each site,
runs there against that site's own data, and only a summary, a
count, a rate, a model's sufficient statistics, travels back to be
combined. No patient-level row ever crosses a site boundary.

The chunk below plays the part of five sites computing their own
30-day event rate and sending back only two numbers each, the
count and the number of events, which is all a fixed-effect
combination needs:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rand <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))
outc <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))

site_summary <- rand |>
  left_join(outc, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  filter(ascertained) |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarise(n = n(), events = sum(event_30d), .groups = "drop")

site_summary
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   site       n events
#>   <chr>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Site A   654    135
#> 2 Site B   536    132
#> 3 Site C   462     98
#> 4 Site D   349     86
#> 5 Site E   268     57

overall_rate <- sum(site_summary$events) / sum(site_summary$n)
overall_rate
#> [1] 0.2238872
```
:::


A coordinating analyst who never sees a single patient's record
can still compute the overall 30-day event rate of
22.4% from these ten
numbers, five counts and five event totals. What a federated
analysis cannot do as easily is anything that needs a joint
distribution across sites, such as an interaction between site and
a patient-level covariate; that kind of question either stays
within one site or is negotiated as a further, specific summary
each site is willing to release, not as row-level data.

### Output disclosure control

A TRE's safe settings keep row-level data from leaving, but a
table of counts can disclose almost as much if a cell is small
enough. The crosstab below, site by race, a real covariate pattern
in the synthetic HF-HOME file, is exactly the kind of table an
analyst would ask to take out of a TRE to put in a report:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
demographics2 <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"),
                          col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
race_tab <- demographics2 |>
  left_join(rand, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  count(site, race)

race_tab |> filter(race %in% c("American Indian or Alaska Native",
                               "Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander"))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 3
#>    site   race                                          n
#>    <chr>  <chr>                                     <int>
#>  1 Site A American Indian or Alaska Native              3
#>  2 Site A Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     8
#>  3 Site B American Indian or Alaska Native              4
#>  4 Site B Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     7
#>  5 Site C American Indian or Alaska Native              5
#>  6 Site C Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     6
#>  7 Site D American Indian or Alaska Native              7
#>  8 Site D Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     5
#>  9 Site E American Indian or Alaska Native              8
#> 10 Site E Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     2
```
:::


Several of these cells hold fewer than ten patients. A table this
small lets anyone who knows that one American Indian or Alaska
Native patient was treated at Site A, perhaps from a referral
pattern or a clinic schedule, now also learn whatever else the
report cross-tabulates by site and race for that row, not because
any identifier survived but because the cell has only one person
in it. **Small-cell suppression** removes the count rather than
the row:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
suppress_small_cells <- function(n, threshold = 10) {
  dplyr::if_else(n < threshold, NA_integer_, n)
}

race_tab |>
  mutate(n_released = suppress_small_cells(n)) |>
  filter(race %in% c("American Indian or Alaska Native",
                     "Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander"))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>    site   race                                          n n_released
#>    <chr>  <chr>                                     <int>      <int>
#>  1 Site A American Indian or Alaska Native              3         NA
#>  2 Site A Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     8         NA
#>  3 Site B American Indian or Alaska Native              4         NA
#>  4 Site B Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     7         NA
#>  5 Site C American Indian or Alaska Native              5         NA
#>  6 Site C Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     6         NA
#>  7 Site D American Indian or Alaska Native              7         NA
#>  8 Site D Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     5         NA
#>  9 Site E American Indian or Alaska Native              8         NA
#> 10 Site E Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander     2         NA
```
:::


Most TREs set their own threshold and their own rule for what
counts as a disclosive cell (a complementary suppression problem
arises when every other cell in a row or column is visible, which
can let a reader back out a suppressed count by subtraction from a
reported total); ten is a common choice but not a universal one,
and the output-check team inside the TRE, not the analyst alone,
signs off on what leaves.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Suppressing the cell and reporting the row and column totals
defeats the suppression.** If the report also states that Site A
enrolled 701 patients in total and gives every other race category
at Site A, a reader recovers the suppressed count by subtraction.
Output checking in a real TRE looks at the whole table a researcher
wants to take out, not one cell at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A trial statistician argues that because the
analysis runs inside a TRE, de-identifying the data first is
unnecessary. Evaluate the argument against @tbl-deident-five-safes.

**Answer.** The argument conflates safe settings with safe data.
A TRE's access controls lower the chance that row-level data leak
out, but they do not lower what a leak, an insider misuse, or an
output that slips past review would expose if it did. De-identifying
the data inside the TRE is still worth doing, because it is the
one safe that protects the data even when one of the other four
fails.
:::

### Exercises

4. The federated computation above sends back `n` and `events`
   per site. A colleague proposes sending `age` and `event_30d`
   for every patient instead, 'to make the combining easier down
   the line'. What has changed, and which Safe in
   @tbl-deident-five-safes does it violate?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Sending patient-level `age` and `event_30d` is no longer a
federated analysis; it is a data export with two columns instead
of all of them, and a quasi-identifier (`age`) travels with an
outcome that many studies treat as sensitive. It violates safe
outputs: the output leaving each site is no longer a checked
summary but row-level data that was never reviewed for disclosure
risk, regardless of how few columns it has.
:::

## Synthetic data and differential privacy {#sec-deident-synthetic}

Every HF-HOME file used so far is itself synthetic, generated by a
script rather than collected from patients, which is why the
chapter can show real-looking de-identification code without
touching anyone's actual record (@sec-deident-worked's opening).
That is a different use of the word from the one in this section.
There, syntheticity is a property of the whole dataset, built once
to stand in for a real trial throughout this book. Here, **synthetic
data** is a disclosure-control technique applied *to* a real
dataset: replace the real records with records drawn from a model
fit to them, so that no released row corresponds to an actual
patient, while the dataset's statistical structure, as much of it
as the model captures, survives for analysis.

### Generating synthetic data

The simplest synthesis shuffles each column independently,
preserving every column's marginal distribution exactly while
destroying any association between columns:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(20260501)
synth_naive <- release_sh |>
  mutate(age = sample(age), sex = sample(sex), zip3 = sample(zip3))

head(synth_naive)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   subject_id age   birth_year sex   race          ethnicity zip3  discharge_year
#>   <chr>      <chr>      <int> <chr> <chr>         <chr>     <chr>          <int>
#> 1 S0001      63          1944 M     Black or Afr… Not repo… 921             2025
#> 2 S0002      81          1960 M     White         Hispanic… 921             2024
#> 3 S0003      69          1953 M     Asian         Not Hisp… 920             2025
#> 4 S0004      74          1971 F     Not reported  Hispanic… 920             2024
#> 5 S0005      73          1952 M     White         Not Hisp… 921             2025
#> 6 S0006      67          1955 F     White         Hispanic… 921             2025
```
:::


Every age, sex, and ZIP prefix in `synth_naive` is a value that
appeared in `release_sh`; none of the three-way combinations need
have appeared together in a real patient. The `synthpop` package
[@nowok2016synthpop] does the same job properly: instead of
shuffling columns independently, it synthesizes them one at a time
in a chosen order, each one modeled on the real values of the
columns synthesized before it (by default with classification and
regression trees), so that the associations among columns are
preserved rather than destroyed (display-only; not installed in
this environment):

```r
library(synthpop)  # display-only; not installed here
synth <- syn(release_sh,
            visit.sequence = c("sex", "age", "zip3", "race",
                               "ethnicity", "discharge_year"))
```

### Judging utility and disclosure risk

A synthetic release is worth nothing if it answers a different
question than the real data would, and it is worth nothing either
if it still points back at a real patient. Both have to be
checked, and neither check is optional.

**Utility** asks whether a model fit on the synthetic data agrees
with the same model fit on the real data. The independent-column
shuffle above fails this badly whenever the relationship of
interest is between two of the shuffled columns, which is usually
exactly the relationship a trial exists to estimate:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = "c", .default = "?"))
trial <- rand |>
  left_join(outc, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  left_join(base, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  filter(ascertained) |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")))

fit_real <- glm(event_30d ~ arm + ef_pct, data = trial, family = binomial)
or_real <- exp(coef(fit_real)["armHome health"])

set.seed(1)
trial_naive <- trial |>
  mutate(arm = sample(arm), ef_pct = sample(ef_pct))
fit_naive <- glm(event_30d ~ arm + ef_pct, data = trial_naive,
                 family = binomial)
or_naive <- exp(coef(fit_naive)["armHome health"])

c(real_odds_ratio = round(or_real, 2),
  naive_synthetic_odds_ratio = round(or_naive, 2))
#>            real_odds_ratio.armHome health 
#>                                      0.86 
#> naive_synthetic_odds_ratio.armHome health 
#>                                      0.99
```
:::


The real data show an odds ratio of
0.86 for home-health visits, consistent with the
protective effect the trial was built to find; the naively
synthesized data show a ratio of 0.99, because
shuffling `arm` destroyed its association with the outcome before
the model ever saw it. `synthpop`'s sequential synthesis exists
precisely to keep this from happening, and its `compare()`
function overlays the two models' coefficients and confidence
intervals so that a utility failure like this one is visible
without hand-rolling the comparison above.

**Disclosure risk** asks the opposite question: whether a record
that was identifiable in the real data is still identifiable, or
nearly so, in the synthetic one. One check is whether a
combination of quasi-identifiers that was unique in the real data
reappears in the synthetic release, a **replicated unique**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
real_unique <- release_sh |>
  add_count(age, sex, zip3) |>
  filter(n == 1) |>
  distinct(age, sex, zip3)

synth_combos <- synth_naive |> distinct(age, sex, zip3)
replicated <- real_unique |> semi_join(synth_combos,
                                       by = c("age", "sex", "zip3"))

c(real_uniques = nrow(real_unique),
  also_in_synthetic = nrow(replicated))
#>      real_uniques also_in_synthetic 
#>               173                65
```
:::


65 of the 173 combinations that
singled out one real patient in `release_sh` also appear somewhere
in `synth_naive`. No synthetic row *is* that patient, but a
released dataset that reproduces their rare combination still
tells an attacker who already suspects that patient was in the
study that the combination was real, which is itself a disclosure.
`synthpop`'s `disclosure()` function computes this and related
measures (display-only), including whether a record's full set of
quasi-identifiers, not just a three-column summary, is replicated.

::: {.callout-important title='Differential privacy'}
k-anonymity (@sec-deident-risk) and the utility and risk checks
above are properties of a particular released *dataset*: run them
again on a different release and the numbers change. **Differential
privacy** [@dwork2006calibrating] is instead a property of the
*mechanism* that produced a result, a mathematically provable bound
on how much that result could possibly have changed had any one
record been added, removed, or altered. A mechanism satisfying
that bound guarantees it for every record, in every dataset it
might ever be run on, before anyone runs it, which is the kind of
guarantee neither k-anonymity nor a synthetic-data utility check
can offer; the latter two show that a given release held up,
without bounding what a different release might do.

The bound is usually met by adding carefully calibrated random
noise to a statistic, tuned so that one record's presence or
absence barely moves the noisy answer. This book treats the idea
conceptually only: calibrating that noise correctly, choosing the
privacy budget (usually called $\epsilon$) that trades accuracy
against protection, and composing many queries without exhausting
that budget are each their own technical literature, well past an
introductory look. What matters for this book is the contrast: the
U.S. Census Bureau adopted differential privacy for the 2020
Census specifically because it could offer that provable bound
across every table the Bureau might publish, not because it was
the most accurate option for any single table. The accuracy a
single table loses is the cost of a guarantee that holds for all
of them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** The naive shuffle preserved every column's marginal
distribution exactly, yet the utility check found it useless.
Why does preserving marginals not preserve utility?

**Answer.** Most analytic questions, including the trial's own,
are about associations between columns, not about any one column's
distribution on its own. Shuffling columns independently guarantees
that each one's distribution is unchanged while guaranteeing, with
the same move, that no two columns are related to each other any
longer. A synthesis has to model the joint distribution, as
`synthpop`'s sequential approach does, to keep what most questions
actually need.
:::

### Exercises

5. Recompute the odds ratio for home-health visits after
   shuffling only `ef_pct` and leaving `arm` as it was in
   `trial`. Compare it with `or_real` and `or_naive` above, and
   explain why shuffling `arm` was the step that mattered.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
trial_partial <- trial |> mutate(ef_pct = sample(ef_pct))
fit_partial <- glm(event_30d ~ arm + ef_pct, data = trial_partial,
                   family = binomial)
c(real = round(or_real, 2),
  ef_pct_only_shuffled = round(exp(coef(fit_partial)["armHome health"]), 2),
  both_shuffled = round(or_naive, 2))
#>                 real.armHome health ef_pct_only_shuffled.armHome health 
#>                                0.86                                0.86 
#>        both_shuffled.armHome health 
#>                                0.99
```
:::


Shuffling only `ef_pct` leaves the odds ratio close to
0.86, because `arm`, the column the research
question is actually about, kept its real association with
`event_30d`. The earlier naive synthesis shuffled `arm` as well,
which is what erased the finding; a covariate's own distribution
can be resampled far more freely than the treatment assignment a
trial exists to evaluate.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; a release is a build
   product.** Write the release as a script from the untouched
   raw file, so that it can be regenerated and audited.
2. **Habit 8: make the quiet failure loud.** Assert the Safe
   Harbor conditions on every release, and compute $k$; a release
   that looks clean is the plausible-number bug of disclosure
   control.
3. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** The releases
   join the crosswalk, the offsets, and the visits with
   `relationship =` and `unmatched = "error"`, so that a missing
   or duplicated patient stops the build rather than leaking or
   vanishing.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins and @sec-why).* Turn the worked example into a
   script, `R/make_releases.R`, that reads the raw HF-HOME files
   and writes the Safe Harbor release, the crosswalk, and the
   linkable release to separate files, with the two Verification
   chunks as assertions. Run it twice in fresh R sessions and show
   that the Safe Harbor release is byte-for-byte identical.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The script needs three things the chapter's code already has: a
fixed seed before each random draw (the crosswalk and the
offsets), the salt read from an environment variable rather than
typed, and the assertions placed before any `write_csv()`, so that
a failed check writes nothing. Compare the two runs with
`tools::md5sum()` on the output files, or with
`identical(readr::read_csv(a), readr::read_csv(b))`. The crosswalk
belongs outside the project directory, or at least outside Git:
it is the one output that must never travel with the compendium,
the reverse of the sharing @sec-why argues for.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code or rule | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Drop direct identifiers | `select(-c(mrn, first_name, last_name, phone))` | Names and numbers in a release |
| Keep the year only | `as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))` | Day-level dates under Safe Harbor |
| Pool ages over 89 | `if_else(age > 89, "90+", as.character(age))` | Identifying the very old |
| Remove their birth year | `if_else(age > 89, NA_integer_, birth_year)` | Undoing the pooling |
| Truncate ZIP codes | `substr(zip, 1, 3)`, then `000` for restricted prefixes | Small-area identification |
| Random subject ID | `sprintf("S%04d", sample(n()))`, crosswalk held back | A derived re-identification code |
| Keyed hash (Expert Determination) | `digest::digest(paste0(salt, mrn), "sha256", serialize = FALSE)` | Losing linkage across extracts |
| Per-patient date shift (Expert Determination) | `date + shift`, one `shift` per patient | Losing intervals |
| Assert no dates remain | `!any(vapply(d, inherits, logical(1), "Date"))` | A date surviving Safe Harbor |
| Measure residual risk | `min(count(d, age, sex, zip3)$n)` | Unique records in a 'clean' release |

: De-identification in practice at a glance.
{#tbl-deident-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-02c}

1. Pooling hides the exact age only if nothing else in the row
   restates it. A birth year beside a discharge year gives the age
   by subtraction, so Safe Harbor removes 'any date element,
   including the year' that would reveal an age over 89, and the
   release sets the birth year to `NA` for those patients and
   asserts that it did.
2. Every combination of age, sex, and ZIP prefix that appears is
   shared by at least one record, which is to say that at least
   one patient is alone in a cell and distinguishable from
   everyone else in the release. $k$ is a minimum, not an
   average; the patient who is alone is identifiable whatever
   the other cells hold.
3. One study-wide offset preserves the differences between
   patients, so a single known true date recovers every other
   date in the release. A per-patient offset keeps each patient's
   own intervals while breaking that chain, at the cost of the
   calendar relationship between patients. Either way the shifted
   dates are full dates, so the release needs an Expert
   Determination.
